coreIdea: Dividing every score by a temperature before the softmax decides how strongly a language model prefers its top word.
title: Temperature decides how sure the next word is
dek: A language model turns scores into chances. Divide the scores by one number first, the temperature, and the model slides from always picking its favourite word to trying almost any.

sections.heading: Scores become chances
paragraphs: At each step a language model gives every possible next word a score. A function called *softmax* turns the scores into chances that add up to 1, and the highest score gets the biggest chance.[[m1]]

sections.heading: One knob for sharpness
paragraphs: Before the softmax, sampling code divides every score by a temperature T. Drag T below 1 and watch the top word take almost everything. Drag it above 1 and the bars even out.

sections.heading: From greedy to adventurous
paragraphs: Close scores make the knob matter more. With five nearly equal scores, T decides whether the model always says the same word or wanders. As T gets close to 0, the model always picks its top word, which is called **greedy decoding**.

figures.title: Temperature sharpens the softmax
figures.caption: Five candidate next words for “The cat sat on the …”. Drag T.
figures.alt: Bar chart of the chance of five next words at temperature 1, with “mat” highest. Lowering T sharpens the bars into one spike on “mat”; raising T flattens them toward equal heights.

figures.title: Close scores, big swings
figures.caption: Five words with nearly equal scores. Small changes in T move a lot of the chance.
figures.alt: Bar chart of five next words whose scores differ by less than one, nearly level at temperature 1. Lowering T toward 0.05 hands almost all of the chance to the first word.

takeaway: Only the gaps between scores matter, measured against the temperature. Divide by a small T and the top word wins outright; divide by a large T and every word gets a chance.

notes.plain: The chance of word i is e raised to its score, as a share of that number added up over every word.

coreIdea: A hot object cools in proportion to how much hotter it is than the room, so the gap shrinks by the same fraction every minute.
title: Why coffee cools fast, then slowly
dek: A hot drink loses heat in proportion to how much hotter it is than the room. That one rule makes the gap shrink by the same fraction every minute.

sections.heading: Heat flows down the gap
paragraphs: A cup at 90 °C in a 20 °C room loses heat quickly. At 25 °C it barely cools. Newton's law of cooling makes this exact: the cooling rate is proportional to the gap between the cup and the room.

sections.heading: The curve
paragraphs: Follow that rule minute by minute and the gap shrinks by the same fraction each minute, so the temperature falls steeply at first and then levels off.[[m1]] Drag the point along time and watch the drop slow down. Raise k, the cooling constant, and the whole curve falls faster.

sections.heading: A half-life for the gap
paragraphs: Because the gap always shrinks by the same fraction, it takes the same time to halve, whatever the starting temperature.[[m2]] A cup at 90 °C and one at 50 °C take the same time to halve their gaps.

figures.title: Temperature over time
figures.caption: The temperature of a cup over an hour. Drag the point, then change k and the starting temperature.
figures.alt: Line chart of temperature against time from 0 to 60 minutes, falling from 90 °C toward a room temperature of 20 °C, steeply at first and then slowly. Raising k makes the fall steeper.

figures.title: Faster cooling, shorter half-life
figures.caption: How long the gap takes to halve, against the cooling constant k.
figures.alt: Line chart of the gap's half-life against the cooling constant k from 0.01 to 0.3 per minute: about 69 minutes at k = 0.01, falling steeply and then flattening near 2 minutes at k = 0.3.

takeaway: Cooling is proportional to the gap, so the gap shrinks by the same fraction every minute. The temperature falls fast, then slowly, and the gap halves in the same time from any start.

notes.plain: The temperature is the room temperature plus the starting gap, and the gap shrinks by the same fraction every minute; k sets how fast.
The gap halves after about 0.69 divided by k minutes, where k is the cooling constant per minute.
